title: Hard and soft light — Image Wiki
text:
Hard and soft light
  Whether shadows have crisp edges or fade gradually. It is decided by one thing — how big the light looks from where the subject is standing.

  
    Termhard light / soft light
    Also calledharsh light, diffused light, light quality
    Not the same aslight direction, light intensity, contrast ratio
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensWhat you can see in the pictureWhat changes when you change itThe same choice indoorsCommon mistakesWhen you want hard light
      
    
  

  Look at any shadow edge in a picture — the shadow a nose casts on a cheek, say. Sometimes it is a knife line: lit, then dark, nothing between. Sometimes it takes a finger's width to fade.
That difference is hard versus soft light, the fastest thing to read in an image once you know to look. A bare bulb is hard; the same bulb behind a shower curtain is soft.


Hard: direct sun, June 1939
Soft: heavy overcast, November 1940


Left: Marion Post Wolcott, church in a corn field, Manning, South Carolina, June 1939. Right: Jack Delano, A square with old houses in an old fishing village, Stonington, Conn., November 1940. Both Library of Congress FSA/OWI Kodachromes, catalogued under their original titles; both public domain.
Same planet, same star, two Kodachrome frames of a wooden building. Left, the sun: half a degree wide, so every solid thing draws a shadow you could trace. The eaves lay a hard-edged band of shade across the boards below them, the tree is a single dark mass, and each corn leaf casts its own little shadow — which is why the field reads as crunchy texture rather than green paint.
Right, the same sun behind a cloud deck. Now the source is most of the visible sky, and there is not one cast shadow in the frame: nothing from the telephone pole onto the white clapboard behind it, nothing from the cars onto the road, only a faint darkening under the eaves. Nothing about the buildings changed. The source got bigger.


Why it happens
One thing decides it: how big the light source looks from where the subject is standing. Not how bright it is, and not what is printed on the modifier.
Stand at a point on someone's cheek and look back toward the light. You can see the whole source, part of it, or none of it. That is the entire mechanism.

Small sourcesun, bare bulb, phone flashedges snap from lit to darkabruptLarge sourcewindow, softbox, overcast skyedges roll from lit to darkgradualfully blockedpartlypartly

Left: the source is effectively a single point. Every spot on the floor either sees that point or it does not — there is no in-between, so the shadow has one crisp edge and the sphere flips from lit to dark along a hard line.
Right: the source is wide. Near the middle of the shadow, both edges of the lamp are blocked — fully dark. Out at the sides, one edge of the lamp is still visible — partly lit. That band of "partly lit" is the soft edge. Widen the source and you widen the band.


A shadow edge is soft because part of the light still reaches it. Nothing more mystical than that.
The sun is the sanity check: 1.4 million kilometres across, 150 million away, so half a degree of sky from here — a pea at arm's length. Hence the hard shadows at noon. Behind a cloud layer the sky itself becomes the source, a hundred degrees wide.

The one number that matters
Apparent size = actual size ÷ distance. A 1-metre softbox one metre away is enormous to your subject and very soft. Drag it back five metres and it is a small light again — hard, and dimmer as a side effect. Same box, opposite result.

What you can see in the picture
Four signs, easiest first:

Shadow edges. Crisp = hard, gradual = soft. The reliable one.
The terminator — where lit turns to unlit on a curved object. Hard light gives a sharp boundary; soft light gives a long roll.
Specular highlights. A small blown-out dot means hard; a broad dim sheen means soft. On skin, glare versus glow.
Texture. Hard light makes every pore and brick edge cast its own shadow; soft light fills them in.

One frame can contain both, and then the edges tell you which source did what.



Vilhelm Hammershøi, Interior, Sunlight on the Floor, 1906 (National Gallery, London). Public domain.
Two sources of very different apparent size, in one room, and you can sort them out by looking at edges. The patch on the floor has crisp boundaries that reproduce the glazing bars of the window: that is direct sun, half a degree wide, projecting the shape of the opening it came through.
Everything else in the picture is lit by the sky through the same window — a source several feet across as the room sees it — and every one of its transitions is a gradual roll: down the panelled wall, around the door frame, across the tablecloth at the left. No traceable edge anywhere on them.


What changes when you change it



You do this
The light gets
Because




Move the source closer
Softer (and brighter)
It covers more of the subject's sky


Move it further away
Harder (and dimmer)
It shrinks toward a point


Bounce off a wall, or fit a bigger box
Softer
The emitting surface is larger


Add a diffuser
Softer only if the diffuser is bigger than the bulb and close to it
The diffuser is the new source


Add a grid, snoot or barn doors
Harder, narrower
The source is cut to a smaller patch



Closer means both softer and brighter — two separate effects arriving together, and people often read the exposure change as softness.
The same choice indoors


Hard: Caravaggio, The Calling of Saint Matthew, 1599–1600
Soft: Vermeer, The Milkmaid, c. 1658


Two paintings, one variable. Both are lit from a high window on the right-ish side; the difference is the size of that window as the figures see it. Both images are in the public domain.
Caravaggio used a small, distant source. Watch the shadow the raised hand throws on the back wall — it has a definite edge, and you could trace it. Faces flip from lit to dark across a couple of centimetres of cheek.
Vermeer used a large one, close by. There is no traceable edge anywhere on the maid: her forehead darkens into her temple over the width of a thumb, and the wall behind her carries a shadow so gradual you have to hunt for where it starts. Same geometry, same sun, different apparent size.


In a render the knob is explicit: the "size" slider on an area light is the softness slider, and a sun light with angular size near zero is the point source in the diagram's left panel.
Common mistakes

"It is a softbox, so it is soft light." Not if it is small or far away. Apparent size is what counts, and the label does not know where you put it.
"Soft means low contrast." Different axes. Soft light with no fill and a black wall behind still goes from bright to nearly black — softly. Hardness is the edge; contrast is the gap.
"Soft means dim, hard means bright." Brightness is intensity and distance. Blinding soft light and feeble hard light both exist.
"Diffusion paper always softens." Only if it becomes a bigger emitting surface than the bulb, which means it has to sit close to the bulb. Taped onto a small flash it barely changes the geometry — you just lose light.
Confusing soft light with a lack of direction. Soft light still comes from somewhere. A big window on the left still puts the shadow side on the right.

When you want hard light
Hard light is not the amateur option — it is a choice with a job:

Drama and graphic shape. Sharp shadows read as harsh and high-stakes, and they become compositional elements in their own right. Film noir is built on it.
Texture as the subject. Weathered wood, sand ripples, cracked paint, muscle definition: raking hard light is the only way to make surface relief visible.
Honesty about the setting. Midday in a desert should look hard.

Soft light is the commercial default not because it is better but because it is forgiving: it hides skin texture, it does not punish a subject for moving 20 cm, and it rarely produces an ugly shadow by accident.

How to check an image in five seconds

Find one clear cast shadow. How wide is the fade at its edge, next to the object casting it?
Find a curved surface. Does it snap from light to dark, or roll?
Find something shiny. Hot dot, or broad sheen?
Do the three answers agree? If one shadow is razor-sharp and another in the same frame is a soft gradient, there are two sources — or the image is a bad composite.


Point 4 earns its keep: mismatched shadow softness between a subject and its background is one of the most reliable tells that an image was assembled from parts, by a person in Photoshop or by a generative model.

  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Light direction
              Where the light sits relative to the subject and to the camera. It decides where the shadows land and how much of the shaded side you get to see, which is what makes a flat picture look solid.
            
          
        
          
            
              Light falloff
              How fast light gets dimmer as it travels away from its source. The useful part is that it changes fastest right next to the lamp and barely at all far away.
            
          
        
          
            
              How to look at an image
              A repeatable way to see what an image is actually doing, instead of only noticing whether you like it.
